background_notes.fact: For real k, s↦exp(-i*k*s) is smooth, has derivative -i*k*exp(-i*k*s), and has complex modulus one. For real x,y, |exp(i*x)-exp(i*y)|<=|x-y|.

grounds.reason: alpha,beta and the integration variables are real; the interval has finite length tau>0.
The integrands are exactly complex exponentials of imaginary multiples of real phases.

background_notes.justification: The real-variable sine and cosine formulas for the complex exponential give smoothness, the displayed derivative, and modulus one. Integrating the derivative of t↦exp(i*t) between x and y and taking its norm bounds the difference by the interval length, since the derivative has modulus one. This is the routine exponential estimate explicitly used in S001.

background_notes.fact: Continuous complex functions on a compact real interval are integrable; the integral is linear and satisfies |integral f|<=integral |f|. For complex C1 functions h,q on [0,tau], integral h*q'=[h*q]_0^tau-integral h'*q. Consequently, for real beta≠0 and q(s)=exp(-i*beta*s), |integral_0^tau h(s)q(s)ds|<=(|h(0)|+|h(tau)|+integral_0^tau |h'(s)|ds)/|beta|.

grounds.reason: tau>0; hcov is an exponential minus its constant average and hence smooth, as is q. The argument restricts this use to beta≠0.
All integrals are over the finite interval [0,tau], and the averaging normalization is 1/tau.

background_notes.justification: Linearity and the norm bound follow from integration of the two real coordinates and the triangle inequality for integral sums; continuity guarantees integrability. Apply the fundamental theorem of calculus to (h*q)'=h'*q+h*q' to obtain integration by parts. Substituting q'=-i*beta*q and |q|=1 gives the stated estimate. Applied to the displayed difference formula for hcov, the same norm bound yields |hcov(s)|<=(|alpha|/tau) integral_0^tau |s-r|dr. At s=0 and s=tau the integral is tau^2/2, giving the exact endpoint sum in S001; for all s it is at most tau^2. Also |hcov'|=|alpha|. These are routine applications along the packet's existing route, with no limit exchange.

background_notes.justification: Multiplicativity and the triangle inequality are the usual absolute-value identities and inequalities; for complex numbers they follow by squaring the modulus and using Re(u*conj(v))<=|u||v|, and the real versions follow by signs. Integer discreteness gives |n|>=1 when n≠0. Ordering four real numbers uses finitely many comparisons, so no compactness or extremum theorem is required. These facts justify the magnitude comparisons, positive divisions and exhaustive pair splits in S002 and S003.
